title: Mechanism versus rate law
promptMarkdown:
For $\ce{2 NO(g) + Cl2(g) -> 2 NOCl(g)}$ the following mechanism is proposed:

- Step 1: $\ce{NO + Cl2 <=>[k_1][k_{-1}] NOCl2}$
- Step 2: $\ce{NOCl2 + NO ->[k_2] 2 NOCl}$

Define the rate as $\tfrac12\,d[\ce{NOCl}]/dt$ throughout and say so.

1. Check that the steps add to the overall equation and name the intermediate.
2. Assume step 1 is a fast pre-equilibrium and step 2 is slow. Derive the predicted rate law and compare it with the experimental law $k_{\text{obs}}[\ce{NO}]^2[\ce{Cl2}]$ from exercise 1; express $k_{\text{obs}}$ in terms of $k_1$, $k_{-1}$, $k_2$.
3. Assume instead that step 1 is slow and step 2 fast. What rate law results, and is it consistent with experiment?
4. Without assuming either limit, apply the steady-state approximation to $[\ce{NOCl2}]$ and derive the general rate law. Show that it reduces to your answers in parts 2 and 3 in the appropriate limits, stating each limit as an inequality between rate terms.
5. Describe an experiment on the model (which concentration to vary, what to measure) that would distinguish the two limits, and say what each predicts.
hintLadder: Each step-2 event produces two molecules of $\ce{NOCl}$, so $d[\ce{NOCl}]/dt = 2k_2[\ce{NOCl2}][\ce{NO}]$; your defined rate is half of that.
In a pre-equilibrium, $k_1[\ce{NO}][\ce{Cl2}] = k_{-1}[\ce{NOCl2}]$; solve for the intermediate and substitute.
The limits are $k_{-1} \gg k_2[\ce{NO}]$ and $k_{-1} \ll k_2[\ce{NO}]$; the apparent order in $\ce{NO}$ differs between them, which is what an experiment can see.

checkExamples.label: correct derivation
checkExamples.text: Adding the steps: NO + Cl2 + NOCl2 + NO → NOCl2 + 2NOCl, i.e. 2NO + Cl2 → 2NOCl; NOCl2 is the intermediate. Rate = ½ d[NOCl]/dt = k_2[NOCl_2][NO]. Pre-equilibrium: k_1[NO][Cl_2] = k_{-1}[NOCl_2], so rate = k_2 k_1 [NO]^2 [Cl_2]/k_{-1} = k_2 K_1 [NO]^2[Cl_2], matching experiment with k_obs = k_1 k_2/k_{-1}. Slow first step: rate = k_1[NO][Cl_2], first order in NO, inconsistent. Steady state: 0 = k_1[NO][Cl_2] − k_{-1}[NOCl_2] − k_2[NOCl_2][NO], so [NOCl_2] = k_1[NO][Cl_2]/(k_{-1} + k_2[NO]) and rate = k_1 k_2 [NO]^2[Cl_2]/(k_{-1} + k_2[NO]). For k_{-1} ≫ k_2[NO] this is the pre-equilibrium law; for k_{-1} ≪ k_2[NO] it is k_1[NO][Cl_2]. Experiment on the model: vary [NO] at fixed [Cl_2]; the steady-state law predicts the apparent order in NO falling from 2 towards 1 as [NO] grows, whereas pure pre-equilibrium predicts order 2 throughout.

checkExamples.label: numbers substituted instead of a derivation
checkExamples.text: With [NO] = 0.1 the rate is 1.8e-4; with n=1 and n=2 and n=3 the law k[NO]^2[Cl2] fits, so the mechanism works.
